newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire currency gains 60 percent against dollar.
newsitem.headline: Zaire currency gains 60 percent against dollar.

text.p: The battered Zaire currency gained 60 percent against the dollar on Monday, the first day of foreign exchange dealing since Laurent Kabila's rebels captured the capital.
Traders on "Wall Street", Kinshasa's outdoor currency black market, were selling wads of Zaires at 70,000 to one U.S. dollar compared with 180,000 on Friday, the eve of the rebel takeover.
The dramatic strengthening was more about a desire to conform with rebel wishes than any sudden change in economic conditions, the traders said.
"This is the rate the liberators want," said Julienne, one of the hundreds of traders, mostly middle-aged women, who operate the currency market in the city centre.
"We know they will kill us if we carry on at the old rate," said Marie-Jose, laughing but clearly concerned about what the new order will bring.
In the seven-month advance westwards across Africa's third biggest country, Kabila has successfully imposed a degree of discipline in Zaire's monetary mayhem.
In provincial cities like Lubumbashi, Goma and Kisangani, the Zaire has settled at 70,000 to the dollar or even firmer.
Kinshasa will be a tougher nut to crack. The vast city of five million bustles with wheelers and dealers and demand for the dollar and other hard currencies is far higher than elsewhere.
"I think they can hold it at around 70,000. It had to come down," said Eric Cordier, manager of Kinshasa's biggest supermarket.

The shop, selling mostly imported goods, was looted by its private security guards on Saturday night, Cordier said. They stole about 20 percent of the stock, worth three to four million Belgian francs ($85,000 to $110,000).

Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) is packed with former Marxists and socialists but so far their economic ideas are fairly free market, diplomats and business people say.

Kabila, who has proclaimed himself president of the country, has remained at his headquarters in Lubumbashi. But the ADFL's secretary-general, Deogratias Bugera, heads a senior advance delegation sent to Kinshasa.
The Alliance officials were due to outline their economic policies to businessmen and heads of state companies and the Central Bank at separate meetings on Monday afternoon.

The Alliance has reverted to the name "Democratic Republic of Congo", scrapped in 1971 by ousted President Mobutu Sese Seko. The currency, baptised the Zaire in the same year, is also due to recover its old name of "Congolese franc".

The traders on Wall Street were managing to part company on Monday with Mobutu's last denomination, the 100,000 Zaire note. But it was selling at a discount with one dollar fetching only 50,000 Zaires.

It met popular resistance when it was introduced last January during the eclipse of Mobutu's 32-year reign. Kinshasa's satirists quickly dubbed it the "prostate" in a cruel jibe about the form of cancer afflicting the 66-year-old former president, now believed to be exile. ($=35.2 Belgian francs)
